subject: maths
title: Solving linear equations

slides.heading: Equations — keeping both sides balanced
slides.body: An equation states that two expressions are equal. Solving means finding the value of the unknown that makes both sides the same. The golden rule is: whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other — every move is a legal operation that preserves the balance. Linear equations (no x² or higher) always have exactly one solution.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: The method — undo operations in reverse order
slides.body: Think of the equation as a series of operations applied to x. To isolate x, undo those operations in reverse order — subtraction undoes addition, division undoes multiplication. If the equation has brackets, expand them first. If x appears on both sides, collect all the x terms on one side before solving.
slides.note: Second concept slide — no formula applies here; method is procedural.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Solve 7x − 1 = 4x + 11.

steps.instruction: Collect all x terms on one side by subtracting 4x from both sides.
Remove the −1 by adding 1 to both sides.
Check by substituting x = 4 into both sides of the original equation.

slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Dividing before subtracting — e.g. solving 3x + 7 = 22 by dividing first: x + 7/3 = 22/3. This leaves a fraction on the left and gives the wrong answer.
mistakes.correction: Always deal with addition and subtraction first (remove constants from the x side), then divide. For 3x + 7 = 22: subtract 7 to get 3x = 15, then divide by 3 to get x = 5.

mistakes.mistake: Moving a term to the wrong side — e.g. for 5x − 3 = 2x + 9, subtracting 3 from both sides instead of adding 3: writing 5x − 3 − 3 = 2x + 9 − 3, giving 5x − 6 = 2x + 6 and x = 4. Check: 5(4)−3=17 ≠ 2(4)+9=17 — that's actually correct here, but the method is flawed.
mistakes.correction: To move −3 to the other side, add 3 to both sides: 5x = 2x + 9 + 3 = 2x + 12. Then 3x = 12, x = 4. The correct route: collect x terms first, then deal with constants.

mistakes.mistake: Expanding a bracket incorrectly before solving — e.g. solving 3(2x − 5) = 9 by writing 6x − 5 = 9 instead of 6x − 15 = 9 (forgetting to multiply the constant −5 by 3).
mistakes.correction: The factor outside the bracket multiplies every term inside: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15. Then 6x − 15 = 9 → 6x = 24 → x = 4.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Golden rule: whatever you do to one side of an equation, do the same to the other side.
keyFacts.examTip: Every step must be a legal operation on the whole equation — adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing both sides by the same value.

keyFacts.fact: Order of solving: expand brackets first → collect x terms on one side → collect constants on the other → divide by the coefficient of x.
keyFacts.examTip: Undo operations in reverse order: addition/subtraction first, multiplication/division last.

keyFacts.fact: If x appears on both sides (e.g. 7x − 1 = 4x + 11), subtract the smaller x term from both sides to get all x on one side before solving.
keyFacts.examTip: Subtract the smaller multiple of x (here 4x) so the remaining x coefficient stays positive — fewer sign errors.

keyFacts.fact: Always check your answer by substituting back into the original equation. Both sides must give the same value.
keyFacts.examTip: If the two sides don't match after substitution, you've made an arithmetic error — recheck each step.

note: keyFacts: 2-4 entries. Exam-precise language. These are what Mabel writes into her notes.
